doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Learning repertoire from the BBC and records before meeting Jimmy
summary: She learned most of her tunes from the BBC and records before she met Jimmy, and briefly retells how she moved from the Guildhall to vaudeville, ENSA, the USO and meeting Jimmy in Belgium.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Oh yeah. Let’s see. What I was going to tell you that . . . I mentioned that . . . you talked about repertoire. Much of your repertoire you learned from Jimmy apparently is what you’re saying.

Well I learned a lot of them before Jimmy. I knew them because all the tunes that were played in this country were played on the BBC. Big bands. Anything I heard on the BBC I could go to the piano and play. And then I had a lot of records that people brought to the house, of Duke and . . . I don’t know how I missed Jimmy, because I remember having records of Sidney Bechet and Muggsy Spanier and all the Benny Goodman groups with Lionel Hampton and Teddy. I spent hours trying to play like Teddy. Art Tatum. And even when I was going to the Guildhall School of Music, I was more into listening to jazz than I really was into the classical end of things, which I was supposed to be working at, but in the end I left and went out with this vaudeville group.
That led to you meeting Jimmy at that point.
Yeah, right. ENSA was the English version. Then I switched to U.S.O. and went to France. I think I must have talked about this already.

That’s where I met Jimmy, was in Belgium when he was . . . he had . . . he was probably drunk. He had . . . I think he volunteered. He didn’t . . . he wasn’t very smart. He didn’t get himself into a band, like a lot of people did, like Artie Shaw and all those people. They’d be in a band. He went and enlisted as a regular G.I. Then when we were in Belgium and somebody heard him play Reveille or something and said, “My God! It’s Jimmy McPartland. We’ve got to get him out of being a soldier and put him in Special Service so he can play.” That’s how we got together. With this little group, going around and entertaining the groups [sic: troops]. They brought him into the U.S.O. group. So that’s how all that happened.
